question: Throughout the EU, Member States address the issue of child protection and the removal of children from families through varied approaches and differing regulations, with some countries not publishing statistics on the reasons for or numbers of children being taken into state care1.

Collecting unified and harmonised statistics in this area would not only enable a comprehensive overview of the reasons for and frequency of such actions, but would also promote greater transparency and comparability between childcare systems in different countries and encourage the sharing of best practices.
This would be beneficial for researchers and experts, who would have access to up-to-date data for analysis and recommendations within their countries, as well as for parents2. 1.
Is the Commission considering the possibility of harmonising data collection on child removals across Member States, including the reasons for and frequency of the removals?

Is the Commission planning to develop proposals for a unified framework that would encourage Member States to collect and share this information, creating a basis for future policy development in child protection?

Would the Commission consider it useful to explore this issue and possibly consult experts, researchers and representatives of Member States so as to better understand the differences in child protection practices across the EU?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.1.

2025) The Commission Recommendation1 on integrated child protection systems is a key deliverable of the EU Strategy on the Rights of the Child and calls on Member States to develop data management methodologies to improve the availability and comparability of data related to child protection through research with the involvement of professionals, public authorities, civil society, families, care givers and children themselves2 with the necessary procedural safeguards and data protection measures in place.

The Recommendation invites Member States to engage in research on violence against children and integrated child protection systems. For the available data to be child-specific, research should also include, in a safe manner, children’s views.

Measures and evidence generated on models for child protection should comply with the principle of subsidiarity and Member States are encouraged to develop and implement plans to improve the quality of their data and to actively share good practices, through the work of the EU Network for Children’s Rights.

Eurostat operates as the EU’s statistical authority in the harmonisation of statistics in close cooperation with national statistical authorities. Eurostat collects data on social protection expenditure3 for family/children benefits, where benefits cover, among others, shelter and board provided to children and families in a permanent basis such as nursing homes and foster families.
